title: Choosing a test
summary: There is no single best memory test. Engineers choose by **coverage**, **test time** and **where** the test runs: in the factory, at every power-on, or in the lab for diagnosis. This topic puts the pieces together and leads to the MBIST hardware that runs the algorithms.
objectives: Weigh test time against fault coverage for a given memory.
Choose suitable tests for production, power-on and diagnosis.
Explain how a March algorithm maps onto MBIST hardware, hard-wired or programmable.

blocks.caption: Example times for one 1 Mi-word memory; a chip tests many memories in parallel

blocks.md: A big SoC has hundreds or thousands of memories. MBIST tests many of them **in parallel**, so the chip's test time is set by the **largest** memories — and by the **power** the chip may draw while all of them run. Tester time costs money on every chip, so a few hundred milliseconds matter.

tabs.label: Production
tabs.md: At **wafer sort** and **final test**: the strongest test the time budget allows — typically a March C− or March SS class algorithm, several data backgrounds, retention pauses, run **at speed** and at several voltage / temperature corners. Fails are logged for **repair** (spare rows and columns).

tabs.label: Power-on / in field
tabs.md: At every start-up, for example in cars: a **short** test (milliseconds), often a March C−-type algorithm, run before the software uses the memory — because a March test **destroys the content**. Periodic tests during operation must save and restore the data or test one block at a time.

tabs.label: Diagnosis
tabs.md: On a few failing chips in the lab: long tests, many algorithms, and a **failure bitmap** (which cells failed in which element). The pattern of fails points to the defect — a whole row, a column, a pair of cells — and helps the factory improve the process.

blocks.md: Every March test maps onto the same few hardware parts:

rows: **comparator**: read data vs expected data → fail flag
**controller**: a state machine that steps through the elements
blocks.caption: From algorithm to hardware

blocks.md: A **hard-wired** controller runs one fixed algorithm — small, but it cannot change after the chip is made. A **programmable** controller reads the algorithm from a small instruction memory or registers, so engineers can switch to a stronger test after silicon if a new fault type shows up. Commercial MBIST tools ship a library of algorithms and offer both kinds.
